Statement 
(a) There is no district in the country which does not have facilities for 
primary education. 
(b) to (d) To ensure universalisation fo elementary education, the 
Government has launched the National Programme of Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan 
under which District Elementary Education Plans are prepared by the districts 
based on the requirements projected. 
Government is also implementing the Mid-day Meal Scheme in all States 
and U.Ts. except Lakshadweep (which has its own scheme) under which 
foodgrain at the rate of 100 grams per child per day is supplied to States for 
provision of a meal to the children in Government, Government-aided and local 
body primary schools as well as, learning centres established under 
EGS&AIE. 
Recently the Constitution (86th Amendment) Act, 2002 has been 
enacted to make Education for Children in the age group 6-14 years a 
Fundamental Right.

THE MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI AJIT SINGH): (a) and (b) 
There is an overall shortage in availability of fodder in the country. This 
shortage aggravates during drought and other natural calamities as 
experienced in the current drought. 
(c) The following arrangements have been made to minimize the feed 
and fodder scarcity: 
(i) The Government of India is supplementing the efforts of State 
Governments in their fodder development programme through its 
Centrally Sponsored Scheme-"Assistance to States for Feed and 
Fodder Development Programme" under which Central assistance is 
provided for establishment of fodder bank and enrichment of

State share basis respectively. 
(ii) Government of India operates fodder farms located in different agro-
climatic zones in the country with the objective to multiply the quality 
fodder seeds to cater the demand to the farmers. 
(iii) The Government is implementing the Central Minikit Testing 
Programme on Fodder Crops. Fodder kits are supplied to the State 
Department of Animal Husbandry and State Dairy Federations for 
onwards distribution to the farmers free to cost. 
(iv) Free transportation facilities for fodder has been given by Railways due to 
drought. 
(v) The Government of Rajasthan and Uttar Pradesh have been delegated 
power under Essential Commodities Act-1955 to regulate the fodder 
prices and restriction on unauthorized hoarding of fodder in order to 
make available more fodder. 
(vi) State practicing combined mechanized harvesting, have been advised 
to stop burning of straw/stovers so that more fodder may be made 
available.

Statement 
(a) Cases of illegal capture, possession and killing of snakes and 
mongoose, for various purposes including for road shows have been reported

(b) Hunting of wild animals, including snakes and mongoose, is 
prohibited under the provisions of The Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972. 
Inciting any animal to fight or bait any other animal is prohibited under the 
provisions of the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act, 1960. 
(c) The violation of provisions of The Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972 
attracts imprisonment upto six years and fine upto twenty five thousand rupees 
or both while the violation of provisions of the The Prevention of Cruelty of 
Animals Act, 1960 attracts imprisonment upto three months and fine upto five 
hundred rupees or both. 
 
(d) Does not arise. 
(e) The Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act, 1960 already provides that 
no person shall exhibit or train any performing animal unless he is registered 
in accordance with the provisions of Chapter V of the Act. Catching of 
snakes is prohibited under The Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972.

*250. SHRI T.S. BAJWA: Will the Minister of ENVIRONMENT AND 
FORESTS be pleased to state: 
(a) the area under forest in Jammu and Kashmir in 1950 and at present; 
(b) whether the area under forest has declined; and 
(c) if so, the steps taken to increase the area under forest in the State? 
THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI T.R. 
BAALU): (a) to (c) A statement is laid on the Table of the House.

RAJYA SABHA [7 March, 2003] 
Statement 
(a) The recorded forest area in State of Jammu and Kashmir in 1950 and at 
present is 20800 Sq. Km. and 20230 Sq. Km. respectively. 
(b) Yes, Sir. The area under forest has declined slightly between the year 
1950 and 2001 by 2.75% of 1950 level. 
(c) Following are the steps taken for conservation and to increase the 
area under forest in various States including Jammu and Kashmir: 
(i) Afforestation programmes are undertaken by State Governments/UT 
Administrations from their own resources as well as with financial 
assistance from Government of India. 
(ii) Joint Forest Management Committees have been set up in States/ UTs 
involving village communities in protection and regeneration of 
degraded forests. 
(iii) A network of protected area has been established. 
(iv) Ministry of Environment and Forests has prepared a National Forestry 
Action Programme for conservation and development of forests.

achieve it. The allocation made for the forests is not even one per cent of the 
total allocations. Sometimes, it is one per cent; sometimes, it is 0.8 per cent.

Rs. 6,700 crores per year, whereas the to tal allocation, for the Centre and the 
States, is only Rs. 1,600 crores. So, where is the possibility of achieving this 
goal?

relating to the forest cover has been decided as a monitorable target; and the 
period in which this target has to be achieved has been compressed to ten years. This 
means that by 2007, we have to achieve a forest cover of up to 25 per cent. In 
the next Plan, we have to see that 33 per cent of the total geographical area is 
brought under the forest cover. For that purpose, unless and otherwise there is 
a provision of Rs. 13400 crores per year—I want to be frank with my friends

Planning Commission, to see to it that, since they have made it a monitorable 
target, proper allocation is made, and definitely not less than Rs. 13400 crores 
per year, for both the Centre and the States. That is what I have requested.

(a) India became a Party to the Montreal Protocol on Substances that 
deplete the Ozone Layer on 17th September, 1992. The Copenhagen Amendment 
to Montreal Protocol which mandates control of Hydro Chloro Fluro Carbon 
(HCFC), Hydro Bromo Fluro Carbon (HBFC) and Methyl Bromide has also 
been approved for ratification.

(b) The important measures initimated by India for phasing out of 
Ozone Depleting Substances (ODS) are:-

(ODS) is under implementation since 1993. 
(ii) The Ozone Depleting Substances (Regulation and Control) Rules, 2000 
have also been brought into force from 19th July, 2000 to control 
production, consumption and trade of ODS. 
(iii) Access to Multilateral Fund for financial and technical support for 
phasing out of ODS. 
(c) The use of the Ozone Depleting Substance, Chloro Fluro Carbon 
(CFC), in manufacture of aerosol products or pressurized dispensers 
(excluding Metered Dose Inhalers for medical purpose) has beeji prohibited

Statement 
Salient features of the National Agricultural Insurance  
Scheme (NAIS) 
(a) States & Areas covered: The Scheme is available to all States/ U.Ts. 
(b) Crops covered: (i) food crops & oilseeds & (ii) annual commercial/ 
horticultural crops (at present eleven crops namely cotton, sugarcane, potato, 
onion, chilies, turmeric, ginger, jute, tapioca, annual banana and 
61 

RAJYA SABHA [7 March, 2003] 
pine apple are covered). Other eligible crops under the group may be covered 
in due course subject to availability of requisite past yield data. 
(c) Farmers covered: Covers all farmers, including sharecropper, tenant 
farmers. Loanee farmers are covered on compulsory basis, while non-loanee 
farmers are covered on voluntary basis. 
(d) Risks covered; Basically all natural non-preventable risks leading to yield 
losses are covered. 
(e) Sum Insured: Sum insured can extend upto value of 150% of average 
yeld. In case of loanee farmers the sum insured is equivalent to at least 100% of 
loan amount availed for the crop. 
(f) Premium rates: Premium rates may range from 1.5% to 3.5% food 
crops & oilseeds and on commercial lines (actuarial basis) for annual 
commercial/horticultural crops. 
(g) Premium subsidy: small/Marginal farmers are eligible for premium subsidy 
@ 50% which is to be phased out on sun-set basis in a period of five years 
subject to review of financial results. 
(h) Nature of scheme: It is a yield guarantee scheme operating on "Area 
approach" basis. If the actual average yield per hectare of the insured crop for 
the defined area (on the basis of requisite number of Crop cutting 
Experiments in the insured season, falls short of specified Threshold yield, all 
the insured farmers growing that crop in the defined area are deemed to have 
suffered shortfall in their yield and the scheme seeks to provide coverage 
against such contingency. 
(i) Risk sharing: Implementing Agency (GIC) shall bear, until transition to 
acturial regime is made, all claims upto 100% of premium for food crops & 
oilseeds and balance claims are shared between Government of India and States 
on 1:1 basis. In respect of annual commercial/horticultural crops, Implementing 
Agency shall bear all claims upto 150% of premium in the first 3 years and 
200% of premium thereafter. 
(]) Corpus Fund: To meet catastrophic losses, a Corpus fund is created 
with contributions from Central Government and participating States on 1:1 
basis.

(d) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE 
(SHRI HUKUMDEO NARAYAN YADAV): (a) Yes, Sir. According to the 
second Advance Estimates released by Government on 10.2.2003, and quoted 
in the Hindu dated 12th February, 2003, the total foodgrains production during 
2002-03 is likely to be 183.17 million tones which is 28.85 m illion tones or

during the monsoon and the post-monsoon period has adversely affected the 
agricultural production during Kharif and Rabi seasons of 2002-03.

influenced by the extent of rainfall and its temporal and spatial spread 
because about 60% of the net area sown is dependent on rains for water. However,

fluctuations. 
In order to further improve the performance of the agriculture sector, the 
Government have taken a number of initiatives such as promotion of 
watershed development programmes, emphasis on developing and increasing 
availability of agricultural credit, Market Information Network, National 
Agricultural Insurance Scheme etc. Besides, the Government also encourage 
farmers to increase production through price policy which includes 
implementation of Minimum Support Price and Market Intervention 
Schemes. Apart from these, the Government have also adopted macro-
management mode for providing assistance to the States. The Macro-
Management Scheme integrates 27 schemes into one for supplementing and 
complementing the efforts of State Governments through work plans. This 
gives flexibility to States to address specific problems faced by them 
depending on local

†1726. SHRI KRIPAL PARMAR: Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is fact that a Bovine Commission, set up for Bovine 
promotion, has submitted its report to Government; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether Government have accepted the recommendations made in the 
report; 
 
(d) if so, by when, and 
(e) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE 
(SHRI HUKUMDEO NARAYAN YADAV): (a) to (e) Yes, Sir. The salient 
features of the recommendations of the National Commission on Cattle (Bovine 
Commission) are annexed as Statement. (See below). An Expert Group headed 
by Joint Commissioner (CBF) in this Department have been constituted to 
examine the recommendations submitted by National Commission on Cattle and 
to suggest measures to implement them. The Group has been asked to submit 
its report by 15th March 2003. After receipt of the report of the Group, further 
follow up action will be taken. 
Statement 
The salient features of the recommendations made by the  
National Commission on Cattle. 
(1) The prohibition for slaughter of cow and its progency should be 
included in the Fundamental Rights to make it enforceable by the 
Court of Law. 
(2) The Constitution should be amended to empower Parliament to enact 
a Central Law for prohibition of slaughter of cow and its progency 
and its transport from one State to other. This may be done by shifting 
the subject to Central list or atleast to the concurrent list in the 
Seventh Schedule of the Constitution. 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
97 

RAJYA SABHA [7 March, 2003] 
(3) Any violation of this law should be made non-bailable and 
cognizable offence and provide for trial by a Session Court. The 
minimum punishment for violation should be three years rigorous 
imprisonment, which may extend to ten years with fine. The onus of 
proof should be on the accused to prove his innocence. 
(4) The Central Government should constitute a permanent National Cattle 
Development Commission or Rashtriya Goseva Ayog for the country 
as a whole to provide it adequate funds for its functioning. 
(5) A separate Ministry for Cattle Preservation and Development should 
be formed independent of the Department of Animal Husbandry. 
(6) Animal Husbandry Department should be re-organized and the 
subject allotted to it should be for preservation and development of 
animals and not for animal food by way of meat etc. 
(7) No financial assistance should be given by the Animal Husbandry or 
Agriculture Department for the construction or maintenance etc. of 
slaughter houses in the country. 
(8) There should be complete ban on the export of beef and veal. 
(9) The Central Government should ensure constitution and functioning 
of Goseva Ayogs in each State and also provide them adequate funds 
for their functioning. These Ayogs should be monitored by the 
Rashtriya Goseva Ayog at the Centre. 
 
(10) Central Cattle Protection—Rapid Task Police Force with regional 
offices in each States should be created. It should have a special force 
deputed on the Kerala and Bangladesh Border to check exodus of 
cattle. 
(11) Appropriate direction may be given under Article 355 of the 
Constitution to the Government of Kerala and north-eastern States to 
enfoce prohibition of slaughter of cow and its progeny. 
(12) Special protection may be given to Kerala to stop receiving cattle from 
neighbouring States for slaughter. 
(13) The cruelty to cattle during their transp~ rt by rail/trucks etc. and 
extraction of milk by giving oxytocin should be prohibited. 
98 

[7 March, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
(14) A circular should be issued by the Government for banning 
production of leather of slaughtered cattle. The export of goods made 
of such leather should be banned. 
(15) Penal law like POTA should be amended to detain smugglers/ mafia 
of cow and its progeny who indulged in large-scale exodus to Kerala 
and Bangladesh. 
(16) Cross breeding from imported cattle like Jersey and their import 
should be prohibited. 
(17) Indigenous breeds should be encouraged and Government should provide 
sizeale financial assistance for their development and preservation 
throughout the country. A National Breeding Policy should be evolved 
and special plans should be developed and implemented. 
(18) The report of the Organic Manure Task Force Committee 2001 should 
be accepted and its recommendations implemented in toto. 
(19) The use of production of chemical fertilizers and chemical pesticides 
should be discouraged. 
(20) The recommendation of the XI Sub-Group (on Meat Sector) set up by 
the Planning Commission for the 10th Plan proposals should be 
rejected outright. 
(21) Gaushalas, Gosadans and Pinjrapoles should be organized through 
voluntary organizations both by Central/State Governments.The 
Government should give financial assistance/ grants for construction 
and maintenance of such Gaushalas and their day-to-day expenses. 
(22) The Information and Broadcasting Ministry should undertake 
programmes for awarenness campaign of qualities and virtues of cow 
milk, cow products etc. 
(23) The State should be asked to ensure production of fodder and feed in 
proportion to cattle population. 
(24) Burning of standing crop residues in States like Punjab and Haryana 
that can be used, as fodder should be made a penal offence. 
99 

RAJYA SABHA [7 March, 2003] 
(25) Fodder Corporation of India should be established with its branches 
in each State on the pattern of the Food Corporation of India. 
(26) Special fodder production drive should be undertaken by the 
Agriculture Universities and Agriculture Ministries in collaboration 
with the Ministry of Environment and Forests. 
(27) The Central/State Governments should subsidies the fodder sale on the 
pattern of subsidy given to people below poverty line form ration 
shops. 
(28) A circular should be issued to the State Government, Gram 
Panchayats & Municipal Committees to regulate and maintain the 
stray cattle. 
(29) Every state must have a breed centre which should concentrate on the 
development of local bread alone. 
(30) The Cattle Laws Enforcement Directorate shoud be constituted which 
shall be incharge of the movement of cows, bulls etc. from place to 
place and State to State. 
(31) Export and Import of beef should be totally banned. 
(32) Cow should be declared as National Animal and killing of cow and 
its progeny should be made constitutional offence. 
Conditions of small and marginal farmers 
1727. SHRI P. PRABHAKAR REDDY: 
SHRI RUMANDLA RAAMACHANDRAYYA: 
SHRI SURESH PACHOURI: 
Will the Minister of AGRICULTRE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware of the pitiable conditions of small and 
marginal farmers leading to distress sale of their products and to suicides in 
extreme cases; 
(b) if so, the details thereof and the reasons therefor; 
(c) whether a study has been conducted by National Sample Survey 
Organisation in this regard; 
100 

[7 March, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
(d) if so, the details of findings; 
(e) whether Government have formulated any plan to offer reliefs to these 
farmers; 
(f) if so, the details thereof and if not, the reasons therefor; 
(g) whether Government propose to waive crop insurance premium for 
them, and 
(h) how the Tenth Five Year Plan addresses to the problems of these 
farmers? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN TH E MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE 
(SHRI HUKUMDEO NARAYAN YADAV): (a) and (b) The main objectives of 
the Government's price policy for agricultural produce are aimed at ensuring 
remunerative prices to the farmers including small and marginal farmers for their 
produce with a view to encourage higher investment and production. The 
Government fixes each season Minimum Support Prices (MSPs) of major 
agricultural commodities and organizes purchase operations through public 
and coperave agencies such as Food Corporation India (F.C.I.-paddy, wheat 
and coarse cereals), Jute Corporation of India (J.C.I.-Jute), Cotton 
Corporation of India (C.C.I.-Cotton), National Agrcultural Cooperative 
Marketing Federation (NAFED-pules and oilseeds) and Tobacco Board (Tobacco), 
besides other agencies designated by the Governments. The designated Central 
Nodal Agencies are required to intervene in the market for undertaking purchase 
operations in case, the prices fall below the MSPs fixed by the Government by 
and large, the wholesale prices of major agricultural commodities are ruling 
above the MSPs fixed by the Government and there are no reports of distress 
sale during the 2002-03 season. 
(c) and (d) The National Sample Survey Organisation (NSSO) has not 
conducted any survey regarding conditions of small and marginal farmers. 
However, a Situation Assessment Survey of farmers is currently being conducted 
by the NSSO.The field work for the Survey commenced in January, 2003 and is 
planned to continue till December, 2003. The report of the Survey is expected 
to be available after about 12 months from the date of completion of field 
work of the Survey, i.e. towards the end of the year, 2004. 
101 

RAJYA SABHA [7 March, 2003] 
(e) and (f) The Department of Agriculture & Cooperation is 
implementing various schemes for increasing agricultural production and 
productivity and they are meant for all categories of farmers. These schemes 
provide assistance in various components and some of the components give 
special consideration to certain category of farmers such as small and 
marginal farmers. 
The Government also implements schemes for price and market support 
which, inter-alia, helps in strengthening the farm income and economic 
conditions of the farmers. These schemes cover all categories of farmers 
including small and marginal farmers. 
(g) There is no proposal under consideration to waive premium for Crop 
Insurance under National Agricultural Insurance Scheme (N.A.I.S.). However, 
there is a provision to provide 50% premia-subsidy to small and marginal 
farmers by the Government. The Premia-subsidy will be phased out over a 
period of five years; 
(h) Schemes providing for special consideration to certain categories of 
farmers like small and marginal farmers are being continued during the Tenth 
Plan. As regards other schemes, the benefits of increase in production and 
productivity in agriculture are expected to accrue to all farmers, including the 
small and marginal farmers.

AND FORESTS (SHRI DILIP SINGH JUDEV): (a) to (d) Ambient air

India's proposals at Johannesburg summit 
†1745. SHRIMATI KUM KUM RAI: Will the Minister of 
ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS be pleased to state: 
(a) the details of proposals submitted by India for securing concessions, 
assistance and consultation from developed countries for 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
118 

[7 March, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
under developed countries in the Earth Summit on practical development recently 
held in Johannesburg; 
(b) whether there was any consensus on these oroposals in the above 
Summite and if so, the details thereof and the way in which they were 
reflected in the declarations and proposals; and 
(c) steps taken by Government in view of these proposals? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF ENVIRONMENT 
AND FORESTS (SHRI DILIP SINGH JUDEV): (a) The Summit started in 
the backdrop of the attempts made by developed countries to dilute the 
principle of common but differentiated responsibilities as agreed at United 
Nations Conference on Environment and Development in Rio de Janeiro in 
1992. India with the help of like minded countries succeeded in making the 
industrialized world reaffirm their commitment to these principles. The other 
equally important concerns which were raised by the developing countries 
were ensuring access for the people to clean water and sanitation facilities, 
increasing access to energy and health services, halting and preventing loss of 
Biodiversity and its sustainble utilization, changing the present unsustainable 
patterns of consumption and production and means of implementation to 
achieve these objectives. The efforts made by various blocks on imposing 
disguised trade barriers in the nature of eco-labeling, life-cycle analysis criteria, 
and inclusion of core labour standards of International Labour Organization 
were successfully countered by the developing countries, 
(b) The Plan of Implementation and Political Declaration issued after the 
Summit has highlighted concerns of developing countries and reflect consensus 
among all countries arrived at the World Summit on Sustainable 
Development.The Plan of Implementation calls for immediate international 
action to tackle these issues. 
(c) The Government regularly monitors its performance against the 
benchmark of annual and Five Year Plans which contain all elements of 
sustainable development. Ministry of Environment and Forests has set up a 
mechanism for follow up action on various decisions taken at the World 
Summit.

country during the last four years and the action taken against the 
organizations/individuals responsible for such imports; and

into the country? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF ENVIRONMENT 
AND FORESTS (SHRI DILIP SINGH JUDEV): (a) Food derived from 
genetically modified organisms (GMOs) is termed as GM food. The GM foods

the Corn Soya Blend (CSB) imported by CARE & CRS through USAID, does

Statement 
Performance Review of Yamuna Action Plan 
General Conclusions 
(1) On the basis of the assessment of the works in the Yamuna Action Plan 
(YAP) towns it is concluded that the YAP is a well-conceived and 
implemented plan which has served the purpose of improving the water 
bodies receiving the wastewaters and the general environment of the 
towns. The following main conclusions have been drawn:— 
(a) Generally all the drains carrying wast waters and polluting the river 
Yumana have been covered but in some towns some drains have been 
left out or only partly intercepted and some new point sources of 
pollution have arisen. However, despite the Extended Phase there are still 
drains in some towns, which remain uncovered. In this connection, by 
way of illustration, the towns of Muzaffarnagar, Yamunanagar, Agra, 
Faridabad can be mentiond. 
(b) STPs are generally performing well but they are under-loaded. 
(c) Power cuts are frequent and sometimes the Diesel Generator sets are not 
able to cope with the failure. 
(d) Water quality testing facilities are generally available. 
(e) Sludge is being used as compost in many places and the farmers are 
themselves picking it up. 
(f) Generally, the Community Toilet Complexes are being managed well. 
However, in some cases, the local population is not utilising the 
facilities of Community Toilets mainly because of levy of high user 
charges. A system of monthly passes for families may be considered 
on charges decided in consultation with the community. Non-
Governmental Ogranisations (NGO) may also be invited to motivate 
the local population. 
(g) The afforestation programme, though small, is generally successful. 
(h) The bathing ghats are popular and are being used. 
139 

RAJYA SABHA [7 March, 2003] 
(i) The acceptability of improved wood-based crematoria is poor except 
at Mathura. 
(j) There is no planned utilisation of the nutrient rich treated effluent. 
(k) Sewer cleaning is in general ad hoc and there is no schedule. No data 
could be made available from local hodies/Nigam about the extent of 
utilisation of sewer cleaning machines. 
(I) The State agencies have been given the responsibility of operation and 
maintenance. However, in UP adequate funds are not provided to the UP 
Jal Nigam for this purpose. 
(m) The enforcement of environmental standards on industry is the 
responsibility of the State Pollution Control Boards (SPCB). In most 
cases the agencies responsible for Operation & Maintenance (O&M) of 
assets created under Yamuna Action Plan (YAP) are not aware of the 
measures taken by SPCB in this regard. 
(n) Some of the Micro/Mini Sewage Treatment Plants have not stabilised. 
Their performance, therefore, can not be evaluated in Delhi. Where the 
data has been collected, it is inadequate to comment on their 
performance. 
(o) The demonstration plants tor disinfection have been set up recently, enough 
time has not passed and it is premature to draw any conclusions. 
General Recommendations 
(a) The discharges not attended under Phase I or those arising after the 
YAP works had been approved need to be covered in the future. 
(b) Regarding cleaning of sewers, the concerned authorities should have 
the equipment and follow the methodology prescribed under the 
CPHEEO Manual on Sewerage. 
(c) Under Phase II of Yamuna Action Plan inclusion of solid waste 
management should also be considered. 
(d) The problems related to supply of power need to be resolved by the 
State Government. 
140 

[7 March, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
(e) Adequate funds need to be provided to UP Jal Nigam for Operation & 
Maintenance (O&M) till the local bodies are in a position to take over 
and maintain them. This needs urgent attention. 
(f) Upfiow Anaerobic Sludge Blanket (UASB) is a new technology. 
Manuals for operation and maintenance of such plants, and indeed of each 
component of the entire system consisting if interception & diversion, 
pumping stations and sewage treatment plants (STP), need to be prepared 
for guidance of maintenance staff and contractor. 
(g) Testing facilities are generally available but in Mathura, Vrindavan and 
Etawah they have not been provided. However, in a majority of 
laboratories trained technical staff is not available. Testing should either be 
given out on contract or a regular training programme or sampling and 
analysis be initiated in an academic/scientific institution to train staff 
who could subsequently do the analysis on a regular basis. 
(h) The polishing pond should have a detention period of two days so that 
the quality of effluent can improve further, algal cells are conserved 
and pisciculture/aquaculture can be promoted. 
(i) The treated effluent is being discharged in to nearby drains. The 
Ministry of Environment & Forests may consider encouraging the State 
Governments to prepare and construct suitable irrigation schemes. 
G) In the UASB sewage treatment plants, the gas should be utilised for 
running the STPs and the pumps. 
(k) The river water quality both upstream and downstream of the town should 
be monitored as in Ganga Action Plan towns. Bio-monitoring should also 
be added. 
(I) The administrative and financial sustainability of YAP works should be 
studied and suitable measures taken. 
Public Participation and Public Awareness 
Public Participation and Public Awareness activities under YAP have not 
been very effective due to various fact ors. One of the major factors for low 
visibility is the fact that the scale of the activities is low and it is 
141 

RAJYA SABHA [7 March, 2003] 
essential that the scale be substantially increased to increase visibility. It can 
be said in the overall assessment that the PA/PP programme was not very 
effective due to various reasons. Some of them are as under: 
(a) The allocations of funds to the non-core activities (low cost sanitation, 
crematoria, river front development) in the YAP is very small 
compared to the core activities (sewage treatment plant, interception 
& diversion). In order to have a visibility and effectiveness an optimal 
investment in non-core activities is essential as it is the non-core 
activity with which normally the general public is associated with and 
can actively participate. 
(b) The means used to reach out to the public are not very effective. It is 
suggested that small films are made to make the people aware and 
publications in local languages should be made in local newspapers, to 
reach the masses. 
(c) For continued success of the YAP, it is essential that project is made 
self-sustaining in the long run. This can happen only when the public is 
willing to share the cost of keeping Yamuna clean with greater public 
awareness and participation.

RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (SHRIMATI JAS KAUR MEENA): (a) to 
(c) The Government of India (GOI)- UNICEF Master Plan of Operations 
(MPO) for the period 2003-07 has been signed on 13th January, 2003. The 
proposed programmes will be implemented in the fields of Education, Health, 
Water and Sanitation, Child Development and Nutrition, Child Protection and 
HIV/AIDS. The objectives of the programme of cooperation include, among 
others, reduction of infant and maternal mortality, reduction of malnutrition 
and protection of children and adolescents from HIV/AIDS. An amount of US 
$400 million has been allocated by UNICEF for the MPO period which

main programmes implemented were in the fields of primary education, 
reproductive and child health, child development and nutrition, child's 
environment (sanitation, hygiene and water supply), child protection, rural 
convergent community action, urban convergent community action and 
advocacy. The programme was completed successfully in December 2002 
with a fund utilization of about 96%.

KATHIRIA): (a) to (c) the Expenditure Reforms Commission in its 9th

Schooling in North Eastern Region 
1786. SHRI KARNE NDU BHATTACHARJEE: Will the Minister of 
HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) details of Government of India's schemes for education to all by 2003 
in the North Eastern Region with particular reference to Assam; and 
(b) whether such schemes are Centrally financed by Government or will it 
be jointly financed by Government of India and the States; if so, the details 
thereof? 
169 

RAJYA SABHA [7 March, 2003] 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (SHRI ASHOK PRADHAN): (a) 
Government of India launched Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan (SSA) for providing quality 
education to all children of the age-group 6-14 in the country, including 
Assam in North Eastern Region, by 2010. One of the goals of SSA and its 
component, District Primary Education Programme (DPEP), is to enroll all 
children of the above said age-group in regular schools or centres under 
Education Guarantee Scheme or Alternative and Innovative Education by year 
2003. DPEP, in the North Eastern region of the country, is in operation only in 
Assam. 
Interventions under SSA and its component, DPEP, include setting up of 
schools/alternative education centres, appointment of teachers, qualitative 
improvement of education, teacher training, academic support to schools and 
alternative education centres, provision of teaching-learning material, construction 
of classrooms and school buildings, setting up of Block and Cluster Resource 
Centres, special focus on girls and disadvantaged groups, integrated education 
of the disabled children. 
(b) SSA is being implmented by the Central and State Governments, of 
North Eastern Region, as also of other states, in partnership with the local 
Government and community, district Elementary Education Plans, prepared 
through community ownership are the basis of the programme implementation. 
The sharing pattern of funding between the Centre and State was 85:15 in the 
9th Plan, is 75:25 in the 10th Plan and would be 50:50 thereafter. 
DPEP, which is in operation in Assam, has a sharing pattern of funding 
between Central and State Government as 85:15. 
The District Elementary Education Plans, under SSA, for the financial year 
2002-03 of all the 78 districts of the North Eastern States, including 23 districts 
of Assam, have been approved for a total amount of Rs. 236.078 crore, which 
include Rs. 150.40 crore for Assam. In addition to this, Annual Work Plan and 
Budget for 9 districts of Assam for a sum of Rs. 50.00 crore have been 
approved under DPEP.

1820.  SHRI GHULAM NABI AZAD: 
SHRI RAJKUMAR DHOOT:

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RAILWAYS 
(SHRI BANDARU DATTATRAYA): (a) to (c) Yes, Sir. Details of two

1. Derailment of 12 coaches of 5959 UP Kamrup Express, between Tihu-
Pathsala stations of New Bongaigaon-Changsari section, Alipurduar 
Division, Northeast Frontier Railway on 10.01.2003. As per provisional 
findings contained in the preliminary Inquiry Report of Commissioner of

coaches of 5960 Down Kamrup Express derailed between Diphu-
Nailalung stations of Dimapur-Lumbding Section, Lumbding 
Division, Northeast Frontier Railway on 20.01.2003. 
(d) Following preventive measures have been taken for the safety of 
passengers: 
(i) A non-lapsable Special Railway Safety Fund of Rs. 17,000/- crore has 
been set up for renewal of over aged assets and for safety 
enhancement works. 
199 

RAJYA SABHA [7 March, 2003] 
(ii) All the Production Units, majority of repair workshops and large 
number of Sheds/Depots have achieved ISO 9002 certification for 
their Quality maintenance system. 
(iii) Procurement of new generation diesel locomotives with enhanced safety 
features such as multi-re-setting vigilance control device, computer 
controlled brake system, extended dynamic brake and creep control to 
avoid wheel slipping. 
(iv) Fitment of micro processor control speed recorders to monitor speed of 
the train. 
(v) Procurement of simulators as training aid to improve training of 
running staff. 
(vi) Odour-cum-fume type hot box detectors are under lab tests for timely 
detection and detachment of hot boxes thereby preventing breakage of 
axle/journals on the run. 
(vii) New wagons being inducted into the system are equipped with more 
reliable Casnub Bogies and Air Brake System. Bogie Mounted Brake. 
System on wagons has also been developed. The use of Composition 
Brake Blocks on wagons is being progressively increased. 
(viii) Improvement in the rolling stock design to reduce the impact of 
accidents and resultant casualties. 
(ix) There has been a progressive increase in the use of Tie Tamping and 
Ballast Cleaning Machines for track maintenance. Track Renewal 
Trains are also being used. 
(x) For monitoring track geometry and running characteristics of the track 
sophisticated track recording cars, oscillograph cars and portable 
accelerometers are being used progressively. 
(xi) For detection of rail fractures/weld failures, adequate double rail Ultra 
Sonic Flaw Detectors have been procured. Self Propelled Ultrasonic 
Rail Testing Cars are being procured. 
(xii) Patrolling of Railway track by gangmen is carried out at vulnerable 
locations during the monsoon, summer and winter. 
200 

[7 March, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
(xiii) The specifications of rail steel have been upgraded and are in 
conformity with the International Union of Railways (UIC) 
specifications. 
(xiv) The track structure is upgraded on a planned basis. 
(xv) To keep the track in good condition, track renewals are carried out 
whenever they become due subject to availability of funds. 
(xvi) Derailment prone four wheeler wagons (CRT wagons) are being 
phased out of service. 
(xvii) Closer liaison is being maintained with the State Police Departments, 
wherever required for prevention of crime on Railway tracks and bridges. 
(xviii) Instructions have been issued to reduce the number of fish plated joints, 
wherever feasible and for burring of two fish bolts, one on each rail, at 
joints located in the stretches considered vulnerable. 
(xix) An anti-theft elastic rail clip and fish bolt fastening is under 
development. 
(xx) Stringent penalty to the extent of dismissal/removal from service is 
being imposed on officials causing serious accidents.

TECHNOLOGY (SHRI BACHI SINGH RAWAT): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) The Centre for Science and Environment, a non-Governmental 
organization, has done the pesticides residues analysis based on the 
European Norms which specifies the limit of 0.0005 ppm (Part Per Million)

equipment like Gas Chromatograph using detectors like Electron Capture

already evolved amendments in Indian Standards for Packaged Drinking 
Water and Natural Mineral Water in order to align them with the world's 
best norms for pesticides residues. They will be implemented after they 
are incorporated in the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 which 
is administered by Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. Ministry of

comments from public to amend the standards of Packaged Drinking

PRIVATE MEMBER'S RESOLUTION 
Need to take Initiative to Unite Non-Aligned Movement Against  
War and for Global Peace 
THE VICE-CHAIRMAN (SHRI SURESH PACHOURI): Now, we take up the 
Private Members' Business (Resolutions). Dr. Dasari Narayana Rao, absent. 
Shri Jibon Roy to move a Resolution urging upon the Government to take the 
initiative to unite the Non-aligned Movement against the war and for global 
peace. 
SHRI JIBON ROY (West Bengal): Mr. Vice-Chairman, Sir, I move the 
following Resolution:— 
"Having regard to the fact that:— 
1. The increasing trend amongst a section of the advanced countries 
270 

[7 March, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
of using their military power to blackmail the economically weaker nations; 
2. their superiority in weaponry, specially the atomic authority being used 
for increasing global exploitation, market expansion and establishing global control 
over scarce raw materials, particularly petroleum; 
3. these countries are forcing the Government to surrender states' control 
over economy and even threatening of military interventions for furthering their 
design; and 
4. Anglo-US threat of war against Iraq has endangered not only the 
sovereignty of a third world nation but has also put a question mark on the role 
of the United Nations, the world body founded after World War-11 for upholding 
mutual respect and world peace; this House expresses its satisfaction that the 
people of India and its polity are by and large united on this issue, calls upon the 
people of India to consolidate themselves and join the worldwide opposition 
against the Anglo-US war threat to Iraq and urges upon the Government to take 
the initiative to unite the Non-Aligned Movement against the war and for global 
peace." 
Mr. Vice-Chairman, Sir, it would have been better had it been a full-fledged 
discussion in this House, and some resolution passed. It could have been 
done through a suo motu statement or a discussion. Now things as they stand 
today, here are as if nothing is happening in the world. Sir, it is dangerous. I 
wish the discussion on the resolution should be over today itself and the hon. 
Minister should make a statement, and, if possible, adopted the Resolution 
even with amendments. An amendment is proposed by my hon. colleague, Shri 
Eduardo Faleiro, and is in the tune with the Resolution. I agree with that 
amendment too. 
The war is almost declared in all its practical purpose. It is being told, day 
in and day out, by the people who profess themselves as the guardian of the 
contemporary civilisation, that they will go for a war, irrespective of any 
resolution adopted in the U.N. Security Council or the U.N.This is a blatant attack 
on the spirit of the formation of the U.N.O. as also the U.N. Charter. It is a 
dangerous thing. We should take this with all seriousness. 
A team of Indian Parliamentarians, under the leadership of Shri 
Basudevacharya, of the other House, and some intellectuals, visited Iraq. Just 
yesterday night they have come back. According to them, 
271 

RAJYA SABHA [7 March, 2003] 
"people have reconciled to the fact that the war was coming, at any moment of 
time we would be bombarded by B2 bombers, next would be carpet bombing all 
over Baghdad and other areas." Three million soldiers are posted around Iraq 
along the borders of Kuwait and others. Saudi Arabia and Turky have not 
agreed to the U.S. base yet. And, the U.S. will bomb from all directions. If that 
happens, millions of people will die. My question is, what are we doing? 
Sometimes, I introspect as to what our political parties, our Parliament, our 
State, our Government are doing. The nearer the danger, the threat, more 
lukewarm is the response. It is dangerous. I question myself. It is, probably, a 
reflection of the decline of our civilisation. It should not have been taken. If it is a 
fact that the Indian people have reconciled with imperialism or if they have 
reconciled with global exploitation and military adventure like this, then it would 
have been a different thing. But to my mind, the Indian people by and large are 
against war, against imperialism and against exploitation. They are for humanity. 
Now it is not getting a vent. When millions of people in europe, even in UK, 
America, New York, Sydney, Australia are marching, we have not called upon the 
people to rise against this threat, an uncivilised act. Where comes the role of 
the Government? It is the duty of the Government to unite people against this. 
As you understand, Sir, it is not a matter of Iraq alone. It is a matter of the 
entire Third World nations. The moment the war starts, the price of petroleum 
will shoot up by 50 to 60 dollars per barrel. It has already gone up by 30 dollars 
per barrel. Our economy, the Third World countries, the people, all are involved in it, 
but it looks that there is no Government at all. Or, if the government is there, they 
do not know that something is happening in the world. The other day our Prime 
Minister was telling, "I feel that the NAM is still having its relevance." I do agree. 
But you go through the Declaration that came out in Kuala Lumpur. It is more an 
advice to Iraq than to the aggressor party. All of us are trembling. We do not 
have backbone. We do not stand up. Sir, if we go through the President's 
Address which was made before a Joint Session of Parliament and which we 
have passed, we find that not a single world was there about Iraq and about 
the war threat. Not a single world! All this reflects on our polity, on our politics, on 
our civilisation and on our vision. Now, Sir, thing is that a war will be there even if 
the UN Inspectors do not find a pencil cutter in Iraq. In that case also, a war will 
take place because it is for some other reasons. The Anglo-US forces, Anglo-
US administration wants to remake the political 
272 

[7 March, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
geography of Arab petroleum producing areas. And they will do it. Thb only 
mistake of Iraq is that they are having a petroleum reserve of about 1000 billion 
barrels. It is a proven reserve.They are having more petroleum which is hot yet 
proven. And that is why that area has got to be captured. Another mistake is that 
it is not Iraq that all other big powers are having their companies in Iraq which are 
raising petroleum, but big companies in america and in England are not engaged 
in petroleum raising in Iraq. And the raising charges vest in Iraq than in any other 
part of the world. This is wrong with Iraq and that is why everyday they are being 
threatened that their country will be invaded. In fact, from the way the U.S. is 
moving to force the 'armament discipline 1 over Saddam Hussain's regime, it 
became clear that it is not for implementation of the U.N. resolution No. 1441. 
Now it is clear. Why they are doing it is also understood by the world nations 
and the world bodies. And, in such a situation, my submission before the 
government is that they have to take a lead to unite the third-world nations. And 
they should explain that the current attack or threat of attack is not against Iraq 
alone. It is a threat against all the weaker nations of the world—third-world 
nations, sometimes, we feel pleasure that the Cold War is over, but, I find, since 
the Cold War has gone, the hot war has come in. The Cold War engulfed the 
entire world. And, this hot war is against the third-world nations. With all 
fanfare, we have been beating the drum of globalisation. Now, the worldwide 
corporatisation has come in. Iraq war is a reflection of the corporatisation move. 
After some time, a day will come when they will corporatise even Oxygen! Sir, 
Oxygen would be marketed in the world! And we would be watching it helplessly. 
Hence, my submission is: Will the Government play its role? Will the 
Government take the leadership of the Non-Alignment Movement, which was 
founded and created under the leadership of Pandit Jawaharlal Nehru, under the 
leadership of India? will they unite the entire third-world nations against this 
attack? And, I urge upon the Government to come forward with a clear-cut 
statement on this question and take the initiative to unite the people in our country. 
By and large, the political parties, in our country, are against the U.S. war against 
Iraq. Representatives from all the political parties, cutting across their ideologies, 
have visited Baghdad—one team was led by the hon. Deputy Chairman, Dr. 
Najma Heptullah. And. in such a situation, the Government should take a sound 
position. Therefore, I request the House, all political parties and the 
Government to accept 
273 

RAJYA SABHA [7 March, 2003] 
this Resolution, if necessary, with amendments, and unite the people against 
this war threat.

international political system, which had evolved during the last 300 years. 
During Eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, when European powers 
dominated all over the world—the entire East and that whole Africa were their 
dominions, their colonies, their empires. At that time, in Europe, they 
maintained a system called 'balance of power 1. 'Balance of power' means if 
Prussia wanted to become stronger, France, Austria and England would unite 
against Prussia. If France becomes powerful, other powerful nations would unite, 
so, somehow the world did not find any power as a Super-Power. That was how 
the 'balance of power' worked. But, when we come to early twentieth century, we

British Empire, which made Great Britain a big power, a world power.There was 
French Empire; there was Dutch Empire; there was Belgium Empire; there was

the multi-polar politics continued till the Second World War. But,

Minister of External Affairs that India considers Iraq a friend. We have had good

Now, Sir, we are confronted with a situation on which the Security Council 
of the United Nations is divided. Certainly, three if not four, perm anent 
members—France, Russia and China—are not supportive of the intended military 
intervention by the United States and United Kingdom, and some ohter countries 
Spain and others to take military action. The-United Kingdom has, of course,

SHRI ASHWANI KUMAR (Punjab): Thank you, Mr.Vice-Chairman, Sir. I 
am, indeed, most grateful for the opportunity to speak on this very important 
subject and on the Resolution of my esteemed friend, Mr. Jibon Roy. I am, indeed, 
grateful to the hon. Minister of External Affairs who has found time to sit right 
through the debate, because, I do believe, irrespective of the number in the 
House the matter is of such grave importance that the hon. Minister must 
respond, after hearing every single hon. Member, who wishes to express himself 
on the subject. I will make a brief intervention and I wish to make three or four 
fundamental points. 
We all know the context in which this Resolution is being debated. We all 
know that the threat of a wide-ranging war loom large on the horizon. As my 
esteemed friend, Shri Nariman said, 'we can hope for the best. But, we fear for 
the worst.' My personal hunch is that irrespective of a very wide and a broad 
consensus of public opinion against a unilateral war, I do believe, we are in for 
one. And, in that context, I would like to raise three or four fundamental 
questions. What is it that causes so much anguish to people across the world at 
the thought of this war? I think, the first and the foremost question is: Are we, 
today, in the 21st Century, succeeding or failing in outlawing a war which does 
not have the sanction of the U.N. and, which is ex-facie in violation of the first 
principles of the U.N. charter? Sir, I remember a quote which I read 
302 

[7 March, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
many, many years ago and it has stayed with me. Mr. yice-chairman, Sir, this 
is a quote of Louis Henkin, who wrote his magnificent book on "How Nations 
Behave." That is the title of the book. And, he said, in his opening remarks, 
"The history of civilization is a progress from force to diplomacy and from 
diplomacy to law." Today, we see a reversal to the first stage when a mighty 
nation could choose the timing of the war, the justification for the war and also 
the consequences of the war. India, whose influence in world affairs, we trace 
back to Pandit Jawaharlal Nehru, which basically, rested or was anchored in its 
moral authority, has to come forward to articulate the conscience of the nation, 
not to exert its force around armaments or around economic power, because 
in that line we are far below. But, I think, at a moral level, we have a voice 
which can hardly be ignored. And, Sir, you are armed with the collective will of 
this nation. You would have noticed that the people of India, speaking through 
their representatives, have spoken in one voice. You, as their Minister, at the 
moment, must emphasise that a war is seen to be morally unjustified. At a 
time, when four Members of the Security Council have cautioned against war, 
when the people of the world have expressed solidarity with the people of Iraq 
in the cause of peace, that is the time, Sir, for us, as a nation, to reassert our 
moral credentials and the moral force of our diplomacy and foreign policy. 
The third question and the third submission that I have is on the question 
of the proportionate or the disproportionate use of force. We have seen, very 
recently, a whole nation-Afghanistan-razed to the ground by the mightiest power 
on earth today, in quest of one terrorist, Osama Bin Ladin. And, look at the 
tragedy, look at the anguish, look at the comic or a tragic laughter-call it what 
you may-that a whole nation is razed and one man is still not caught! Nobody 
even knows whether he is dead or alive. This only shows the limitations of war. 
It shows the limitation of the use of force. Sir, you are too knowledgeable a 
person for me to remind that the Second World War owed its origins to the 
humiliating peace inflicted on the vanquished through the Treaty of Versailles. 
I hope, Sir, that the so-called war to weed-out terrorism eventually should not, 
and I pray and I hope that it will not become, a reason for another global 
conflict. I must also, at the same time, caution against a strident attitude even 
against the US position because we 
303 

RAJYA SABHA [7 March, 2003] 
have been victims of terror. We know what terrorism can do to economies, 
what it can do to nations. We know that we are facing a real threat from cross-
border terrorism. Therefore, if we can find a balance between a principled 
reservation against unilateral use of force and the imperative to strengthen a 
world conscience against terrorism, it would eventually ensure to the benefit of 
India. And, that, Sir, is going to be the test of your Foreign Policy. That is going 
to be the test of India's intervention at this very critical hour in the world. {Time-
bell) I would only hasten to add, before I conclude, that we don't really have to 
be defensive when it comes to principles. I know, Sir, that it would be naive on 
anybody's part to say that we can afford to be compulsively, and by habit, on 
the wrong side of the United States. We •cannot. We do recognise the merits. 
We do recognise the benefits and advantages of working together with the 
United States, insofar as our critical interests are concerned. But when it comes to a 
position of principle, when it comes to the assertion of moral authority, on which 
our Foreign Policy has been founded, starting from the time of Pt. Jawaharlal 
Nehru, India cannot dock; India cannot compromise; India cannot wait. 
In conclusion, I would make a fervent appeal to you, to the Government of 
India, and personally to you. Please do take a leadership role in seeking to avoid 
the war; history will always recognise, then, the pre-eminent role which India 
has played. Thank you very much. 
SHRI V.V. RAGHAVAN (Kerala): Thank you, Mr. Vice-Chairman, Sir. I 
congratulate my colleague, Shri Jibon Roy, for bringing this most burning issue 
before the world today for our consideration. I hope, this House of the matured 
parliamentarians can adopt this unanimously. I cut short my speech because 
we have to adopt it within time. The United States of America is not only 
challenging the world body of UN Security Council, but their war cry is also 
against the whole of humanity. The situation is getting worse day-by-day. Mr. 
Powell goes on declaring that the US will not wait for anybody's consent. It will 
act on its own. That clearly spells their aggressive arrogance. This attitude is 
not alone in regard to war against Iraq, but on all international issues, 
confronting the world today. For lack of time, I need not.elaborate them. Iraq is 
fully cooperating with the UN Inspection Mission. Mr. Blix has gone on record 
that Iraq has destroyed, and is destroying the weapons which the UN 
Commission wanted to. In the Security Council,

Mighty nations, like France, Germany, Russia and China are against this 
unilateral action of America. Not only that, a mighty mass upsurge is taking 
place in the world over, including the United States of America and England. Sir, 
about 20 lakhs of people participated in the historical march against war, in

Washington. The people of America declare that this war is not for American

wholeheartedly, stand by the people of Iraq. Our voice should be firm against

Sir, we must stand by the emerging new world, which is against war and is 
for peace. This emerging world is not only against war, but it is also against 
the American attempt to dominate the world, both militarily and economically. 
Our hon. Minister knows well, through their various agencies, what the 
economic domination by the Americans mean. So, a new world is emerging 
against this economic domination. So, a new world, which is against war and is for

the course we can adopt. It has been our course throughout history. So, in this 
critical stage we must stand up, and raise our voice. Our voice is a very 
powerul voice. Our voice should be against the American attempt's to wage a 
war on the whole of humanity. Thank you.

this House that, fortunately, Foreign

what has been stated here, and what the stated policy of the Government is, 
there is no difference, there is no divergence. It might be the case that some 
hon. Members will express it in a certain language; some others will express it 
in a certain language; some others will express it in certain other language. 
Even here, we notice the difference in the refinement of language. But, once 
again, Mr. Vice-Chairman, Sir, though the situation is developing very fast 
now, as President Bush said in a speech which he gave at the press 
conference that he addressed a little while ago, that we are in the final stages 
of diplomacy, what will be the situation over the next few days, is something 
which I would not venture to predict in this House, at this point of time. Now, in 
this fast developing situation, at this point of time, if I were to once again 
reiterate the policy of the Government, what would I like to say. 
The First point is that, we remain entirely committed to a peaceful 
resolution of this particular issue. India has always said from every platform, in 
every conversation, in every dialogue, publicly and privately, that we want a 
peaceful resolution; we want a diplomatic resolution, which means what? It means 
that we are against war; we are against a military conflict. 
The second point is that the UN Resolution 1441 was a unanimous 
Resolution, it was even supported by a country like Syria, something which I 
pointed out when we had a debate on Iraq the last time. What

does it say? And it is salutary for us to take note of the Resolution. After many 
paragraphs, it says:"... decides that Iraq has been, and remains in material 
breach of its obligations under relevant Resolutions, including Resolution 687 
of 1991, in particular through Iraq's failure to cooperate with the United Nations' 
inspectors and the IAEA, and complete the actions required under paragraphs 8 to 
13 of Resolution 687 of 1991." That Iraq has been, and remains in material 
breach; a Resolution, which was unanimous; a Resolution which has been 
accepted by Iraq. 
In the next paragraph, what does it say? It says: "A final opportunity to 
comply with its disarmament obligations under the relevant UN Resolutions." 
Suppose Iraq had not accepted this Resolution, or these Resolutions, then, we 
would be, perhaps, discussing here, whether we should be with Iraq; whether it 
should accept or not accept. But, Iraq has accepted all these Resolutions. It 
says, this is a final opportunity to comply with the disarmament order. And, 
naturally, warns that serious consequences will follow, if there is a further 
material breach. Now, therefore, compliance by Iraq of these resolutions, full 
and effective compliance, is something, which is inherent in the situaiton, and 
this is an obligation, which even Iraq does not deny. But whether there has 
been a further material breach or not on the part of Iraq is a determination, which the 
Security Council of the United Nations has to make.Therefore, what is the third 
principle? The first principle of our policy is, peaceful resolution.The second 
principle is, Iraq should comply. The third principle, therefore, flowing from this, is 
that whatever further decision has to be taken, should be taken multilaterally, 
through the United Nations Security Council. This is what we have said, and this 
means that we are against unilateral action. It means that we are against action, 
which is outside of the United Nations Security Council. I know that some 
statements have been made to the contrary, with or without the United 
Nations. But we have stated our position very, very clearly that it should be 
through the United Nations Security Council. 
The fourth point, which we have, in consideration of the people of Iraq, 
upon which Shri Fali S. Nariman and ohers were speaking, that in view of the 
sufferings of the people of Iraq, in view of the plight to which they have been 
reduced, we have always said that once Iraq complies with these resolutions, 
and is not found to be in further material breach, then the sanctions, which have 
been imposed on Iraq, should be lifted.
